policy_name: One Big Beautiful Bill Act 2025, Section 100001 ("Coast guard assets necessary to secure the maritime border and interdict migrants and drugs")
question: What reporting requirements and notifications are mandated by this section, and to which committees of Congress must they be submitted?
answer_1:
1. The Commandant is required to provide a report under section 11217 of the James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023 (Public Law 117-263) to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate before any funds appropriated under paragraphs (1) and (2) of subsection (a) can be obligated or expended. (f)(2)
2. The Commandant is required to notify the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate not less than 1 week prior to taking any procurement actions impacting estimated costs or timelines for acquisitions or procurements funded with amounts appropriated under this section. (g)
3. The Commandant is required to submit a detailed expenditure plan, including projected project timelines for each acquisition and procurement funded under this section and a list of project locations to be funded under paragraphs (8) and (9) of subsection (a) to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate not later than 90 days after the date of enactment of this Act. (h)
4. None of the amounts provided in this section may be obligated or expended during any fiscal year in which the Commandant is not compliant with sections 5102 and 5103 (excluding section 5103(e)) of title 14, United States Code. (f)(1)

Sources:
- Public Law 117-263, James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023
- Title 14, United States Code, sections 5102, 5103, 1105, 11217, 1131, 1132, 1133, 1151(b)
answer_2: 1) The Commandant must provide a report required under section 11217 of the James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023 (Public Law 117-263) to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate before paragraphs (1) and (2) of subsection (a) can be obligated or expended. 2) The Commandant shall notify the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate not less than 1 week prior to taking any procurement actions impacting estimated costs or timelines for acquisitions or procurements funded with amounts appropriated under this section. 3) The Commandant shall submit a detailed expenditure plan, including projected project timelines for each acquisition and procurement funded under this section and a list of project locations to be funded under paragraphs (8) and (9) of subsection (a) to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate not later than 90 days after the date of enactment of this Act.

policy_name: One Big Beautiful Bill Act 2025, Section 100001 ("Coast guard assets necessary to secure the maritime border and interdict migrants and drugs")
question: Explain the circumstances under which the President can authorize an exception regarding the construction of Coast Guard vessels in US shipyards, and what information must be provided to Congress in such a case?
answer_1:
The President can authorize an exception regarding the construction of Coast Guard vessels in US shipyards under section 1151(b) of title 14, United States Code. This exception is applicable to any Coast Guard vessel, or the hull or superstructure of such vessel for which funds are appropriated under paragraphs (4) through (7) of subsection (a) of the provided context. In such a case, no funds shall be obligated until the President submits to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate a written explanation of the circumstances requiring such an exception in the national security interest. The explanation must include:

1. A confirmation that there are insufficient qualified United States shipyards to meet the national security interest without such exception.
2. Actions taken by the President to enable qualified United States shipyards to meet national security requirements prior to the issuance of such an exception.

Source: Relevant section: 1151(b) of title 14, United States Code, as cited in the provided context.
answer_2: The President can authorize an exception under section 1151(b) of title 14, United States Code, for any Coast Guard vessel, or the hull or superstructure of such vessel for which funds are appropriated under paragraphs (4) through (7) of subsection (a) of the given context. In such a case, no funds shall be obligated until the President submits to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate a written explanation of the circumstances requiring such an exception in the national security interest. This explanation must include confirmation that there are insufficient qualified United States shipyards to meet the national security interest without such exception, and actions taken by the President to enable qualified United States shipyards to meet national security requirements prior to the issuance of such an exception. (Document ID: Context provided)

policy_name: Maryland  H 1128  (Talent Innovation Program and Fund )
question: What are the key components of the Talent Innovation Program, including its administration and pilot program focus?
answer_1:
1. The Talent Innovation Program is a program established in the Maryland Department of Labor to increase access to high-quality job training (11-1602(A)(3)). 2. The Division of Workforce Development and Adult Learning and the Governor's Workforce Development Board jointly administer the Program (11-1602(A)(2)). 3. The Program focuses on increasing access to job training in prominent and emerging industry sectors, including cybersecurity, healthcare, biotechnology, manufacturing, and artificial intelligence (11-1602(A)(3)(I)-(V)). 4. The Program may conduct pilots, convene key stakeholders, and conduct research to develop and support new talent financing approaches (11-1602(B)). 5. The Program shall establish an initial pilot program that focuses on the cybersecurity sector by supporting job training through expansion of regional cyber ranges (11-1602(C)).

Sources:
- Annotated Code of Maryland (2016 Replacement Volume and 2023 Supplement), Article – Labor and Employment, Section 11–1601 through 11–1604
- Annotated Code of Maryland (2021 Replacement Volume and 2023 Supplement), Article – State Finance and Procurement, Section 6–226(a)(2)(ii)189., 190., 191.
answer_2: 1) The Talent Innovation Program is a job training initiative established in the Maryland Department of Labor. 2) The Division of Workforce Development and Adult Learning and the Governor's Workforce Development Board jointly administer the Program. 3) The purpose of the Program is to increase access to high-quality job training in prominent and emerging industry sectors, including cybersecurity, healthcare, biotechnology, manufacturing, and artificial intelligence. 4) The Program may conduct pilots, convene key stakeholders, and conduct research to develop and support new talent financing approaches. 5) The initial pilot program focuses on the cybersecurity sector by supporting job training through expansion of regional cyber ranges, a recognized method for developing talent and meeting the skill needs of the cybersecurity industry.

policy_name: Maryland  H 1128  (Talent Innovation Program and Fund )
question: How is the Talent Innovation Fund structured and what types of expenditures are permitted from it?
answer_1:
The Talent Innovation Fund is structured as a special, nonlapsing fund that is not subject to § 7–302 of the State Finance and Procurement Article (Annotated Code of Maryland, 2021 Replacement Volume and 2023 Supplement, Article – State Finance and Procurement, Section 6–226(a)(2)(ii)191.). The Fund consists of money appropriated in the state budget to the Fund, grants and donations to the Fund, interest earnings of the Fund, and any money from any other source accepted for the benefit of the Fund (Annotated Code of Maryland, 2021 Replacement Volume and 2023 Supplement, Article – Labor and Employment, Section 11–1603(E)).

Expenditures from the Talent Innovation Fund may be made for the following purposes:

1. Providing grants to entities, including employers, institutions of higher education, tax-exempt organizations, public agencies, local workforce development boards, and registered apprenticeship sponsors, and residents of the state, for costs including support services, subsidized wages, grantees' administrative costs, and training (Annotated Code of Maryland, 2021 Replacement Volume and 2023 Supplement, Article – Labor and Employment, Section 11–1603(F)(1)(I)).
2. Providing matching funds to secure donations or grants to the Fund (Annotated Code of Maryland, 2021 Replacement Volume and 2023 Supplement, Article – Labor and Employment, Section 11–1603(F)(2)).
3. Providing funding for the Program and other talent finance mechanisms, such as a pay-it-forward program, approved by the Division and the Board (Annotated Code of Maryland, 2021 Replacement Volume and 2023 Supplement, Article – Labor and Employment, Section 11–1603(F)(3)).
4. Paying expenses for administrative, actuarial, legal, and technical services for the Program (Annotated Code of Maryland, 2021 Replacement Volume and 2023 Supplement, Article – Labor and Employment, Section 1
answer_2: The Talent Innovation Fund is a special, nonlapsing fund established in the Maryland Department of Labor. It is not subject to § 7–302 of the State Finance and Procurement Article. The Fund consists of money appropriated in the state budget, grants and donations, interest earnings, and any other money accepted for its benefit. Expenditures from the Fund may be made for grants to entities, administrative costs, funding for talent finance mechanisms, and administrative, actuarial, legal, and technical services for the Program. (11–1603, Annotated Code of Maryland)

policy_name: Maryland  H 1128  (Talent Innovation Program and Fund )
question: What are the reporting requirements mandated by this legislation to ensure transparency and accountability of the Talent Innovation Program and Fund?
answer_1:
The legislation mandates the Department of Labor to report on Program activities and use of the Talent Innovation Fund on or before January 1 each year, beginning in 2025. The report should be submitted to the Governor and, in accordance with § 2–1257 of the State Government Article, to the President of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Delegates (11–1604(B)).

Citation: Annotated Code of Maryland (2016 Replacement Volume and 2023 Supplement), Article – Labor and Employment, Section 11–1604(B).
answer_2: 11-1604(B) of the Annotated Code of Maryland requires the Department to report on Program activities and use of the Fund to the Governor and the President of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Delegates on or before January 1 each year, beginning in 2025, in accordance with § 2-1257 of the State Government Article.

policy_name: AI Innovation and Development for Efficiency Act of 2024
question: What specific actions will the National Science Foundation (NSF) take under the AIDE Act of 2024 to support the development and expansion of AI-enabled efficient technologies?
answer_1:
The National Science Foundation (NSF) will take the following actions under the AIDE Act of 2024 to support the development and expansion of AI-enabled efficient technologies:

1. Support merit-reviewed and competitively awarded research on the development or expansion of AI-enabled efficient technologies (Section 2(b)(1)).
2. Consider projects that include efficient technology that focuses on building new smart technologies to support critical infrastructure efficiency, minimizing pollution and greenhouse gas emissions from critical infrastructure sectors, and upgrading existing constructions and infrastructure to be more efficient (Section 2(b)(2)).
3. Include an impact assessment conducted by the researcher that evaluates the energy consumption of the artificial intelligence-enabled efficient technology in each research project supported by the NSF (Section 2(b)(3)).
4. Give special consideration to research conducted at EPSCoR institutions (Section 2(b)(4)).
5. Report to Congress on the feasibility for research opportunities, including with relevant Federal agencies and private sector critical infrastructure providers, to improve the development and integration of artificial intelligence-enabled efficient technologies, as well as any recommendations that could facilitate and improve communication and coordination among the NSF, relevant Federal agencies, and the private sector (Section 2(c)(1)).
6. Report to Congress on the results of the research supported under this section not later than 4 years after the date of enactment of this Act (Section 2(c)(2)).

Sources:
- AIDE Act of 2024 (Public Law 118-123)
- 42 U.S.C. 1862g (Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Research)
answer_2: 1) The NSF will support merit-reviewed and competitively awarded research on the development or expansion of AI-enabled efficient technologies, including in areas such as smart grids, mobility or transportation, agriculture, waste reduction, emissions reduction, and resource conservation (SEC. 2(b)(1)(A)). 2) The NSF may also assess the feasibility of safe and reliable adoption of AI-enabled efficient technologies into critical infrastructure and research on the effectiveness of expanding public understanding, development, or adoption of these technologies (SEC. 2(b)(1)(B) and (C)). 3) The NSF will give particular consideration to projects that focus on building new smart technologies to support critical infrastructure efficiency, minimizing pollution and greenhouse gas emissions from critical infrastructure sectors, and upgrading existing constructions and infrastructure to be more efficient (SEC. 2(b)(2)). 4) Each research project supported by the NSF under this subsection will include an impact assessment conducted by the researcher that evaluates the energy consumption of the AI-enabled efficient technology (SEC. 2(b)(3)). 5) The NSF will give special consideration to research conducted at EPSCoR institutions (SEC. 2(b)(4)).

policy_name: AI Innovation and Development for Efficiency Act of 2024
question: Beyond the specified areas (smart grids, mobility, etc.), what other types of research projects related to AI-enabled efficient technologies would be eligible for funding under the AIDE Act of 2024?
answer_1:
Beyond the specified areas (smart grids, mobility, agriculture, waste reduction, emissions reduction, and resource conservation), other types of research projects related to AI-enabled efficient technologies that would be eligible for funding under the AIDE Act of 2024 could include:

* Development of AI-enabled efficient technologies in areas such as manufacturing, construction, and energy storage.
* Research on the use of AI for demand response and energy management in buildings and homes.
* Development of AI-enabled systems for monitoring and optimizing the efficiency of existing infrastructure, such as water distribution networks and transportation systems.
* Research on the use of AI for predicting and mitigating the impacts of natural disasters on critical infrastructure.
* Development of AI-enabled systems for monitoring and managing the environmental impacts of infrastructure projects, such as assessing the potential for habitat destruction or water pollution.

These types of research projects would be eligible for funding under the AIDE Act of 2024 if they meet the criteria specified in the Act, including being merit-reviewed and competitively awarded, and critically considering minimizing emissions, securing clean air and water, building climate and community resiliency, promoting healthy food, and other sustainability pillars.

Citations:

* AIDE Act of 2024, Section 2(b)(1)(A)
* AIDE Act of 2024, Section 3(a) definition of "efficient technology"
answer_2: Research projects related to AI-enabled efficient technologies that are not specifically listed in the AIDE Act of 2024, such as those in manufacturing, healthcare, or energy storage, would be eligible for funding under the act if they meet the criteria of being merit-reviewed, competitively awarded, and focused on the development or expansion of AI-enabled efficient technologies (Section 2(b)(1)).

policy_name: AI Innovation and Development for Efficiency Act of 2024
question: Who are the primary stakeholders, beyond the NSF and Congress, that the AIDE Act of 2024 aims to engage in the development and implementation of AI-enabled efficient technologies, and how will this engagement occur?
answer_1:
The AIDE Act of 2024 aims to engage the heads of other relevant Federal agencies (Sec. 2(b)(1)) and private sector critical infrastructure providers (Sec. 2(c)(1)(A)) in the development and implementation of AI-enabled efficient technologies. The engagement is expected to occur through consultation with these entities (Sec. 2(b)(1)) and the Director's recommendations for facilitating and improving communication and coordination among the National Science Foundation, relevant Federal agencies, and the private sector (Sec. 2(c)(1)(B)).

Citation: AIDE Act of 2024, Sec. 2(b)(1), Sec. 2(c)(1)(A), Sec. 2(c)(1)(B)
answer_2: The AIDE Act of 2024 aims to engage the heads of other relevant Federal agencies and private sector critical infrastructure providers in the development and implementation of AI-enabled efficient technologies. This engagement will occur through consultation with these entities, as the Director of the National Science Foundation is required to consult with them when supporting merit-reviewed and competitively awarded research on the development or expansion of these technologies (SEC. 2(b)(1)). The Director is also required to consider any recommendations that could facilitate and improve communication and coordination among the National Science Foundation, relevant Federal agencies, and the private sector to effectively develop and implement AI-enabled efficient technologies (SEC. 2(c)(1)(B)).

policy_name: Vermont Agency of Digital Services AI Inventory report
question: Explain the key recommendations for maintaining and updating the AI inventory, as proposed by the Agency of Digital Services.
answer_1:
The key recommendations for maintaining and updating the AI inventory, as proposed by the Agency of Digital Services, are as follows:

1. Inventory Maintenance:
   - The Inventory of Artificial Intelligence Usage should be maintained by the Division of Artificial Intelligence within the Agency of Digital Services.
   - The Agency of Digital Services recommends that this inventory be updated as new systems and capabilities are implemented and reviewed for completeness and accuracy annually.

2. Remediation Measures:
   - If an AI system is identified as problematic based on third-party bias testing or other issues, the Agency of Digital Services recommends a suite of possible remediation measures. These measures may include process changes upstream or downstream of the AI system, changes to the AI system itself, or decommissioning all or part of the AI system if continued use would have significant adverse effects or erode trust in government institutions.

3. Inventory Changes:
   - The scope of the inventory should be limited to products the state procures, develops, maintains, influences, or oversees, as well as any systems that are deemed to pose a potential risk to the state or Vermonters.
   - The elements collected in the inventory should include monitoring in place, monitoring results, remediation applied, independent decision-making capabilities, and agencies using the system. Instead of focusing solely on third-party bias testing, the Agency of Digital Services recommends adding elements on outcome monitoring.

Sources:
- 3 V.S.A. § 3305: https://legislature.vermont.gov/statutes/section/03/001/0003305
- National Institute of Standards and Technologies (NIST): https://www.nist.gov/
answer_2: 1. The Inventory of Artificial Intelligence Usage should be maintained by the Division of Artificial Intelligence within the Agency of Digital Services (ADS). ADS recommends that this inventory be updated as new systems and capabilities are implemented and reviewed for completeness and accuracy annually (I.II.A). 2. ADS recommends a suite of possible remediation measures depending on the nature and impact of the issue identified. These include process changes upstream or downstream of the AI System, changes to the AI System, or decommissioning all or part of the AI System if necessary (I.II.B). 3. ADS suggests expanding the scope of the inventory to products the state procures, develops, maintains, influences, or oversees, as well as any systems that are deemed to pose a potential risk to the state or Vermonters (I.II.C.1). Lastly, ADS recommends adding elements on outcome monitoring, specifically Monitoring In Place, Monitoring Results, Remediation Applied, Capable of taking independent action, and Independent Decisions to the inventory (I.II.C.2).

policy_name: Vermont Agency of Digital Services AI Inventory report
question: Summarize the proposed changes to the scope and elements collected within the AI inventory, highlighting the rationale behind these adjustments.
answer_1:
The proposed changes to the scope and elements collected within the AI inventory aim to refine the focus and improve the effectiveness of the inventory.

1. Scope: The proposed change in scope recommends using the narrower definition of Artificial Intelligence System as defined in 3 V.S.A. § 3305, rather than the broader definition of "Automated Decision System." This adjustment is intended to exclude numerous apps, algorithms, spreadsheets, and personal productivity tools that present minimal risk to the state. The inventory will now focus on products the state procures, develops, maintains, influences, or oversees, as well as any systems that are deemed to pose a potential risk to the state or Vermonters.

2. Elements Collected: The proposed changes to the elements collected within the AI inventory aim to provide more comprehensive and actionable information.

   a. Bias Testing: Instead of focusing solely on 3rd party Bias Testing, the inventory will now include elements on outcome monitoring. This change is based on the recommendation by the National Institute of Standards and Technologies (NIST) to continuously monitor system outcomes, as an AI which passes bias testing may behave in biased ways depending on implementation details.

   b. Independent Decision Making: The inventory will now focus on the autonomy of the system, rather than whether the system is used for independent decision-making powers. This change is intended to better reflect the goal of AI systems, which is to make some level of decision.

   c. Agencies using the system: The inventory will now identify the agencies directly using the system. This change is intended to provide more transparency and accountability.

Citations:
- 3 V.S.A. § 3305: https://legislature.vermont.gov/statutes/section/3305/003/00001
- National Institute of Standards and Technologies (NIST): https://www.nist.gov/
answer_2: The proposed changes to the AI inventory include narrowing the scope to products the state procures, develops, maintains, influences, or oversees, as well as any systems that are deemed to pose a potential risk to the state or Vermonters (C.1.1). Additionally, the elements collected will be expanded to include continuous monitoring of system outcomes (C.2.2) and the autonomy of the system (C.2.4). These adjustments aim to ensure comprehensive coverage of AI systems and to focus on the system's behavior and decision-making capabilities. (C.2.2, C.2.4)

policy_name: Vermont Agency of Digital Services AI Inventory report
question: Describe the different remediation measures suggested for addressing problematic AI systems, including examples of how these measures could be applied in specific scenarios.
answer_1:
The report recommends several remediation measures for addressing problematic AI systems in the State of Vermont. These measures can be categorized as follows:

1. Process changes upstream of the AI System: These changes aim to adjust the data input into the system or divert cases with certain characteristics to a different system to remediate issues. For example, if an AI is showing unexpected behavior based on counties with small populations, the county could be set to "Rest of Vermont" for cases where the county is not Chittenden. If an AI is showing unexpected behavior on cases for families with more than 4 children, those cases could be diverted to a manual review system.

2. Process changes downstream of the AI System: These changes add controls downstream of the AI system to address issues that appear sporadically. Depending on the nature of the impact, automated review to detect known problematic patterns could be sufficient. In other cases, selecting cases known to be at higher risk of issues for additional employee review could be a good option. Creating an easy appeal process might also be the most appropriate solution. For example, if an AI is showing infrequent unexpected behavior on cases for families with more than 4 children, an employee could review those determinations before providing the information to the case worker.

3. Changes to the AI System: In some cases, the AI may need to be retrained. This is especially likely if the input or process has evolved from the original design. In some cases, adding some training examples may be sufficient, in other cases the model may need more extensive redesign. If continued use of the AI system would have significant adverse effects or erode trust in government institutions, the most appropriate course may be to decommission all or part of the AI system.

Citations:
- National Institute of Standards and Technologies (NIST): https://www.nist.gov/
- 3 V.S.A. § 3305: https://legislature.vermont.gov/statutes/section/03/001/003305

For more information on the AI Inventory and the report's recommendations, please refer to the document ID: AI-Inventory-Report-2022.
answer_2: The document suggests three types of remediation measures for addressing problematic AI systems: (1) Process changes upstream of the AI System, such as adjusting data input or diverting cases with certain characteristics to a different system (examples provided are for an AI showing unexpected behavior based on counties with small populations or cases for families with more than 4 children); (2) Process changes downstream of the AI System, including automated review to detect known problematic patterns, employee review, or creating an easy appeal process (examples provided are for an AI showing infrequent unexpected behavior on cases for families with more than 4 children); (3) Changes to the AI System, such as retraining or decommissioning the system if continued use would have significant adverse effects or erode trust in government institutions (not provided).

policy_name: Advancing Digital Freedom Act of 2024
question: What are the key areas of focus for the Coordinator for Digital Freedom as defined by this Act?
answer_1:
The key areas of focus for the Coordinator for Digital Freedom, as defined by this Act, are:

1. Improving the state of digital freedom globally (Sec. 4(a)(1)).
2. Ensuring digital freedom remains a foremost foreign policy priority of the United States Government (Sec. 4(a)(2)).
3. Coordinating responses to concerning trends impacting digital freedom (Sec. 4(a)(3)).
4. Engaging foreign governments, nongovernmental organizations, and other actors to defend digital freedom against digital authoritarianism and other authoritarian approaches to governance and usage of technology (Sec. 4(b)(1)).
5. Supporting multilateral efforts to protect and reinforce information integrity within the context of respect for freedom of expression (Sec. 4(b)(2)).
6. Advancing the development and maintenance of technology that is designed, governed, and deployed in manners consistent with democracy, the rule of law, and human rights (Sec. 4(b)(3)).
7. Promoting digital inclusion across the digital space (Sec. 4(b)(4)).
8. Engaging and advancing discussions to promote the democratic governance of artificial intelligence and the implications of artificial intelligence governance on human rights and democracy (Sec. 4(b)(5)).
9. Leading efforts within the Department of State to continue publishing guidelines for protecting digital freedom across the cyberspace, including through the Risk Management Profile for Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, as well as the Roadmap for Building Civil Resilience to the Global Digital Information Manipulation Challenge (Sec. 4(b)(6)).
10. Making recommendations regarding opportunities to advance digital freedom internally within the Department of State, as well as through diplomatic engagements with foreign countries (Sec. 4(b)(7)).

Citation: Advancing Digital Freedom Act of 2024, Sec. 4(a), (b)
answer_2: 1) Improving the state of digital freedom globally, 2) Ensuring digital freedom remains a foremost foreign policy priority of the United States Government, 3) Coordinating responses to concerning trends impacting digital freedom, 4) Engaging foreign governments, nongovernmental organizations, and other actors to defend digital freedom against digital authoritarianism, 5) Advancing the development and maintenance of technology that is designed, governed, and deployed in manners consistent with democracy, the rule of law, and human rights, 6) Promoting digital inclusion across the digital space, 7) Engaging and advancing discussions to promote the democratic governance of artificial intelligence and the implications of artificial intelligence governance on human rights and democracy, and 8) Leading efforts within the Department of State to continue publishing guidelines for protecting digital freedom across the cyberspace. (Sec. 4 of the Act)

policy_name: Advancing Digital Freedom Act of 2024
question: What specific threats to digital freedom will be analyzed in the annual report required by this Act?
answer_1: The annual report required by this Act will analyze specific threats to digital freedom globally, including digital authoritarianism and threats to democracy, censorship and propaganda, threats to information integrity, threats to digital inclusion, threats to privacy in the digital space, and risks to responsible management of artificial intelligence and democratic governance of artificial intelligence (Sec. 5(b)(1) of the Advancing Digital Freedom Act of 2024).
answer_2: The annual report required by this Act will analyze concerning trends impacting digital freedom globally, including digital authoritarianism and threats to democracy, censorship and propaganda, threats to information integrity, threats to digital inclusion, threats to privacy in the digital space, and risks to responsible management of artificial intelligence and democratic governance of artificial intelligence. [SEC. 5(b)(1) of the Advancing Digital Freedom Act of 2024]

policy_name: Advancing Digital Freedom Act of 2024
question: Beyond the explicitly stated duties, what latitude does the Coordinator for Digital Freedom have in their role?
answer_1: The Coordinator for Digital Freedom has some latitude in their role, as specified in Section 4(c) of the Advancing Digital Freedom Act of 2024. This section allows the Coordinator to carry out other duties that the Secretary of State may assign (U.S. Congress, 2024). However, the specific duties and responsibilities of the Coordinator are outlined in Section 4(b) of the Act, which includes engaging foreign governments, nongovernmental organizations, and other actors to coordinate efforts to defend digital freedom, advancing the development and maintenance of technology that is designed, governed, and deployed in manners consistent with democracy, the rule of law, and human rights, and promoting digital inclusion across the digital space, among others (U.S. Congress, 2024).
answer_2: Beyond the explicitly stated duties, the Coordinator for Digital Freedom has latitude to carry out other duties that the Secretary of State may assign (SEC. 4(c)). This implies that the Coordinator may be tasked with additional responsibilities related to digital freedom as deemed necessary by the Secretary of State.

policy_name: West Virginia H 3214 (Road Optimization Assessment Data Pilot Program)
question: What is the intended outcome of using predictive analysis derived from the Road Optimization and Assessment Data Road Pilot Program?
answer_1:
The intended outcome of using predictive analysis derived from the Road Optimization and Assessment Data Road Pilot Program is to render a predictive analysis of roads and highways that results in preventive maintenance for the roads and highways, rather than reactive maintenance. This is based on the rules promulgated by the Commissioner of Highways as stated in section (c)(10) of the bill.

Citation: West Virginia Legislature, "Road Optimization and Assessment Data Road Pilot Program" (2023), §17-2A-25(c)(10).
answer_2: The intended outcome of using predictive analysis derived from the Road Optimization and Assessment Data Road Pilot Program is to render a predictive analysis of roads and highways that results in preventive maintenance for the roads and highways, rather than reactive maintenance (§17-2A-25(c)(10)). This is achieved by collecting data using Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI), GPS positioning, laser measuring systems, videos, and a Reflectometer system, and processing the data twice per year for three years to create a baseline for road condition assessment based on Division of Highways standards and the ASTM D6433-11 Standard Practice (§17-2A-25(c)(1-9)). The ultimate goal is to use this data to proactively maintain roads and highways, improving their overall condition and contributing to the economic and industrial growth and development of the state (§17-2A-25(a)(1)).

policy_name: West Virginia H 3214 (Road Optimization Assessment Data Pilot Program)
question: Explain the data collection and assessment process that the Commissioner of Highways must establish through rules for the Road Optimization and Assessment Data Road Pilot Program.
answer_1:
The Commissioner of Highways must establish rules for the Road Optimization and Assessment Data Road Pilot Program that include the following data collection and assessment process:

1. Collection of data: Employees of the Division of Highways must drive all roads in Monongalia and Preston Counties to capture data. The data collection process will utilize GPS positioning and Geotagged positioning to indicate road geometry and curvature. Laser measuring systems, including video, will be used to longitudinally profile the roads, identify and measure cracks, pavement distress, including potholes, patching, cracking, road shoulder issues, canopy brush, and drainage issues. Videos of the roads will also be used for imagery, as well as for documenting canopy brush, drainage, and the use of a Reflectometer system to check the reflectivity of painted lines.

2. Post data capture processing: After data capture, post data capture processing will be required to create a baseline for road condition assessment based on Division of Highways standards and the ASTM D6433-11 Standard Practice for Roads and Parking Lots Pavement Condition Index Surveys.

3. Frequency of data collection: The data gathering and processing must occur twice per year (spring and fall) for three years.

4. Comparison of changes in road conditions: The data gathered should compare the changes in road conditions such as deterioration of roads from previous condition, average daily traffic, and heavy truck traffic if information is available.

5. Predictive analysis: Ultimately, the data gathered should be used to render a predictive analysis of roads and highways that results in preventive maintenance for the roads and highways, rather than reactive maintenance.

Citations:
- West Virginia Code, §17-2A-25 (2023)
- ASTM D6433-11 Standard Practice for Roads and Parking Lots Pavement Condition Index Surveys (2011)
answer_2: The Commissioner of Highways must establish rules for data collection and assessment in the Road Optimization and Assessment Data Road Pilot Program. The rules should include using Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to assess roads, collecting data from Monongalia and Preston Counties, and having employees drive all roads to capture data using GPS, laser measuring systems, and videos. The data should be processed to create a baseline for road condition assessment based on Division of Highways standards and ASTM D6433-11. The data should be captured and processed twice per year for three years, and the ultimate goal is to use the data for preventive maintenance. (Source: West Virginia Code, §17-2A-25)

policy_name: West Virginia H 3214 (Road Optimization Assessment Data Pilot Program)
question: What specific types of data and technologies are mandated for use in assessing road conditions within the Monongalia and Preston Counties pilot program?
answer_1:
1. The Road Optimization and Assessment Data Road Pilot Program mandates the use of Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to assess the conditions of roads in Monongalia and Preston Counties (§17-2A-25(c)(1)).

2. The program requires the use of GPS positioning and Geotagged positioning to indicate road geometry and curvature (§17-2A-25(c)(5)).

3. Laser measuring systems (including video) capable of longitudinal profiling, identifying and measuring cracks, pavement distress, including potholes, patching, cracking, road shoulder issues, canopy brush, and drainage issues are mandated for use (§17-2A-25(c)(6)).

4. Videos of the roads are required for pavement distress imagery, as well as for documentation of canopy brush, drainage, and the use of a Reflectometer system to check the reflectivity of painted lines (§17-2A-25(c)(7)).

5. Post data capture processing is required to create a baseline for road condition assessment based on Division of Highways standards and the ASTM D6433-11 Standard Practice for Roads and Parking Lots Pavement Condition Index Surveys (§17-2A-25(c)(8)).

6. The pilot program data capturing and processing is required to be done twice per year (spring and fall) for three years, and to compare changes in road conditions such as deterioration of roads from previous condition, average daily traffic, and heavy truck traffic if information is available (§17-2A-25(c)(9)).

7. Ultimately, the data gathered is to be used to render a predictive analysis of roads and highways that results in preventive maintenance for the roads and highways, rather than reactive maintenance (§17-2A-25(c)(10)).

Citation: West Virginia Legislature, 2023, Code of West Virginia, 17-2A-25.
answer_2: The pilot program mandates the use of Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to assess the roads. It also requires the use of GPS positioning and Geotagged positioning, laser measuring systems (including video) for longitudinal profiling, identifying and measuring cracks, pavement distress, road shoulder issues, canopy brush, and drainage issues. Videos of the roads are used for pavement distress imagery, canopy brush, drainage documentation, and the use of a Reflectometer system to check the reflectivity of painted lines. Post data capture processing is required to create a baseline for road condition assessment based on Division of Highways standards and the ASTM D6433-11 Standard Practice for Roads and Parking Lots Pavement Condition Index Surveys. The data capturing and processing is to be done twice per year (spring and fall) for three years.

policy_name: New Hampshire HB 1432 (Deepfakes)
question: What specific activities related to deepfakes are prohibited under this act, and what are the associated criminal and civil penalties?
answer_1:
1. Under this act, it is a class B felony to knowingly create, distribute, or present any likeness in video, audio, or any other media of an identifiable individual that constitutes a deepfake for the purpose of embarrassing, harassing, entrapping, defaming, extorting, or otherwise causing any financial or reputational harm to the identifiable person (RSA 638:26-a II).

2. If a person's violation of the above provision results in an identifiable individual's arrest based on the content of the deepfake, that person shall be guilty of a separate offense, also a class B felony, and liable to the identifiable individual for their legal expenses and the costs of their defense, or to the state of New Hampshire for the same if the identifiable individual is indigent and the cost of defense has been borne by the state of New Hampshire (RSA 638:26-a III).

3. A person may bring a civil action against any person who knowingly uses any likeness in video, audio, or any other media of that person to create a deepfake for the purpose of embarrassing, harassing, entrapping, defaming, extorting, or otherwise causing any financial or reputational harm to that person, for damages resulting from such use (RSA 507:8-j II).

4. This act does not apply to certain entities and uses, such as bona fide news reports, election communications, satire or parody, and the impersonation of another person without reliance on artificial intelligence (RSA 638:26-a IV, RSA 507:8-j III).

5. The provisions of this act are severable, meaning if any provision or application is held invalid, that invalidity shall not affect other provisions or applications that can be given effect without the invalid provision or application (RSA 638:26-a V, RSA 507:8-j IV).

6. The secretary of state shall not accept the registration of any person, partnership, firm, or corporation that has been convicted of an offense under RSA 638:26-a or found liable under RSA 507:8-j related to their lobbying (RSA 15:
answer_2: 1) The act prohibits knowingly creating, distributing, or presenting any likeness in video, audio, or any other media of an identifiable individual that constitutes a deepfake for the purpose of embarrassing, harassing, entrapping, defaming, extorting, or otherwise causing any financial or reputational harm to the identifiable person (RSA 638:26-a II). 2) Violations of this provision result in a class B felony (RSA 638:26-a II). 3) If a violation results in an identifiable individual's arrest based on the content of the deepfake, the violator is guilty of a separate offense (RSA 638:26-a III). 4) A person may bring a civil action against any person who knowingly uses any likeness in video, audio, or any other media of that person to create a deepfake for the purpose of embarrassing, harassing, entrapping, defaming, extorting, or otherwise causing any financial or reputational harm (RSA 507:8-j II). 5) Civil penalties include damages resulting from such use (RSA 507:8-j II).

policy_name: New Hampshire HB 1432 (Deepfakes)
question: How does this act define 'deepfake' and 'artificial intelligence,' and what are the key elements of these definitions that determine the scope of the law?
answer_1: The act defines 'deepfake' as a video, audio, or any other media of a person in which his or her face, body, or voice has been digitally altered so that he or she appears to be someone else, he or she appears to be saying something that he or she has never said, or he or she appears to be doing something that he or she has never done (RSA 243:1, II.b). The act defines 'artificial intelligence' as the ability of a machine to display human-like capabilities for cognitive tasks such as reasoning, learning, planning, and creativity. AI systems may adapt their behavior to a certain degree by analyzing the effects of previous actions and operating under varying and unpredictable circumstances without significant human oversight (RSA 243:1, I.a). The key elements of these definitions that determine the scope of the law are the digital alteration of a person's likeness, the intent to deceive, and the use of AI technology.
answer_2: This act defines 'deepfake' as a video, audio, or any other media of a person in which their face, body, or voice has been digitally altered so that they appear to be someone else, say something they haven't said, or do something they haven't done (243:1, I.b). 'Artificial intelligence' is defined as the ability of a machine to display human-like capabilities for cognitive tasks such as reasoning, learning, planning, and creativity (243:1, I.a). The key elements of these definitions that determine the scope of the law are the digital alteration of a person's likeness and the intent to cause harm or deception.
